actions.name: Numeric pain rating and pain character review
actions.result: Patient rates pain 7/10 at rest, deep boring epigastric/upper abdominal pain radiating to mid-back, worse after meals and when lying flat, partially relieved by sitting forward. Breakthrough pain to 9/10 occurs 2-3 times daily.

actions.name: Opioid regimen and adherence review
actions.result: Prescribed oxycodone IR 5 mg every 4 hours as needed; patient reports taking only 2 doses per day (morning and night) rather than as needed every 4 hours, skipping daytime doses even when pain is severe. No prior opioid exposure before this prescription 6 weeks ago.

actions.name: Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS) screen
actions.result: Pain 7/10, tiredness 7/10, nausea 3/10, depression 5/10, anxiety 6/10, drowsiness 2/10, appetite loss 8/10, wellbeing 7/10, shortness of breath 1/10, constipation 8/10.

actions.name: Bowel function and constipation screen
actions.result: No bowel movement in 5 days; prior baseline was every 1-2 days. Reports hard, infrequent stool when passed, abdominal bloating, no nausea/vomiting currently, no blood per rectum reported. Not currently on any scheduled bowel regimen.

actions.name: Camera inspection of abdomen
actions.result: Visible distension of upper abdomen, no visible masses or discoloration, patient winces on self-palpation of right upper quadrant/epigastrium, no rebound reported by patient, no visible jaundice on camera lighting.

actions.name: Camera inspection of skin and sclera for jaundice
actions.result: No scleral icterus or skin yellowing visible on video under room lighting; patient and caregiver confirm no color change noted at home either.

actions.name: Home vital signs reported by caregiver
actions.result: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, Temp 97.9°F (36.6°C), RR 16, home pulse oximeter SpO2 95% on room air.

actions.name: Functional status assessment (ECOG/Karnofsky)
actions.result: ECOG performance status 3: limited self-care, confined to chair or bed more than 50% of waking hours, requires help with bathing and dressing.

actions.name: Review latest CT abdomen/pelvis report
actions.result: CT abdomen/pelvis shows new hepatic lesions consistent with progressive metastatic disease; pancreatic head mass stable in size; no new biliary ductal dilation.

actions.name: Review oncology note on treatment plan
actions.result: Oncology note documents discussion of second-line gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel alternative or FOLFIRINOX-based regimen; patient has not yet decided; oncologist estimates median survival benefit of second-line therapy is modest (weeks) given declining performance status.

actions.name: Review advance directive status in chart
actions.result: No advance directive, living will, or healthcare surrogate designation on file. Code status not documented.

actions.name: Review recent comprehensive metabolic panel
actions.result: See CMP report: calcium, creatinine, liver enzymes as detailed in artifact; mild transaminase elevation, bilirubin normal.

actions.name: Depression and anxiety screen (brief)
actions.result: Patient endorses low mood most days related to loss of independence and worry about being a burden; denies active suicidal ideation; reports anxiety about pain control and about family conflict over treatment decisions.

actions.name: Caregiver burden and support check
actions.result: Son is primary caregiver, lives 20 minutes away, works full time; patient observes he seems exhausted and overwhelmed but she has not asked him directly how he is coping; no other local family support.

actions.name: Self-reported sedation/cognition check (opioid safety)
actions.result: Patient is alert, oriented, converses clearly, no excessive daytime sedation reported by caregiver, no confusion or hallucinations noted.

actions.name: Goals, values, and illness understanding exploration
actions.result: Patient demonstrates accurate understanding that cancer has worsened despite chemotherapy; she articulates that she values clarity, control, and dignity over prolonging time at the cost of being 'foggy' or dependent; has not shared this directly with her son.

artifacts.title: CT Abdomen/Pelvis with Contrast
artifacts.author: Tampa Radiology Group
artifacts.body: FINDINGS: Pancreatic head mass measures 3.1 x 2.8 cm, stable compared to prior study. New hypodense hepatic lesions are seen in segments IV, VI, and VII, the largest measuring 2.4 cm, consistent with new metastatic disease not present on prior imaging 10 weeks ago. No biliary ductal dilation. No ascites. Mild periportal lymphadenopathy, stable. IMPRESSION: Interval progression of metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma with new hepatic metastases.

artifacts.title: Oncology Follow-up Note
artifacts.author: Dr. Anjali Mehta, Medical Oncology
artifacts.body: Ms. Castellanos seen in follow-up after 3 cycles of gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel. CT shows new hepatic metastases consistent with disease progression. Discussed second-line options including FOLFIRINOX-based regimen or continuation of gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel with dose modification. Reviewed that given declining performance status (ECOG 3) and modest expected benefit (median progression-free survival on second-line therapy in similar patients is measured in weeks to a few months), risks of further myelosuppression and hospitalization are significant. Patient requested time to think it over and discuss with family. Referred to palliative care for symptom management and goals-of-care discussion prior to treatment decision.

profile.encounterType: goals-of-care conversation and symptom management visit

facts.chart: Patient presents for palliative care consult after oncology referral, reporting ongoing upper abdominal pain and uncertainty about next steps in treatment.
facts.says: My oncologist sent me to see you. I have this pain in my stomach that goes to my back, and frankly, I'm not sure what I want to do next about the chemotherapy.

facts.chart: Deep, boring epigastric pain radiating to back, 7/10, worse postprandially and when supine, improved partially by sitting forward.
facts.says: It's a deep, gnawing pain right here under my ribs that goes straight through to my back. It's worse after I eat, and worse lying down flat.

facts.chart: Takes oxycodone 5mg only twice daily rather than every 4 hours as prescribed, due to fear of dependence and cognitive fogginess.
facts.says: I only take that oxycodone pill twice a day, when I truly can't bear it. I don't want to become one of those people who can't function without pills.

facts.chart: No bowel movement in 5 days, baseline every 1-2 days; attributes it to not eating much and being less active.
facts.says: I haven't had a bowel movement in five days. I just thought it was because I'm barely eating.

facts.chart: Unintentional weight loss of approximately 9 kg over 10 weeks.
facts.says: I've lost about twenty pounds. None of my clothes fit anymore.

facts.chart: Spends most of the day seated in a chair; requires assistance with bathing and dressing; was fully independent 3 months ago.
facts.says: I used to be on the bench five days a week. Now I can barely get myself dressed without help.

facts.chart: Mild intermittent nausea, markedly reduced appetite, no vomiting.
facts.says: Food just doesn't appeal to me anymore. I feel a little sick sometimes but I haven't thrown up.

facts.chart: Denies shortness of breath, chest pain, or cough.
facts.says: No, my breathing's been fine. No chest pain, no cough.

facts.chart: Denies yellowing of skin or eyes, denies dark urine or pale stools.
facts.says: No, I haven't noticed any yellow color anywhere, and my urine looks normal.

facts.chart: Reports low mood related to loss of independence and fear of being a burden to her son; denies suicidal ideation.
facts.says: I feel low most days now. I hate needing help for things I used to do myself. But I'm not thinking of hurting myself, if that's what you're asking.

facts.chart: Son strongly advocates for continuing aggressive treatment, tells patient to 'keep fighting.'
facts.says: My son keeps telling me I have to keep fighting, that I can't give up. He means well, but...

facts.chart: Privately wishes to stop chemotherapy and focus on comfort at home but has not disclosed this to her son.
facts.says: If I'm honest with you - and I haven't said this to my son - I don't want more chemotherapy. I want to be at home, comfortable, for whatever time I have left.

facts.chart: Fears disappointing or hurting her son by expressing her true wishes; worried he will see it as giving up on her or on him.
facts.says: He's already lost his father. I don't know how to tell him I'm ready to stop without him thinking I'm abandoning him too.

facts.chart: Values mental clarity, autonomy, and dignity; explicitly states she does not want to spend remaining time 'foggy' or dependent on others for basic care if it can be avoided.
facts.says: I spent my career thinking clearly and making decisions. I don't want to spend my last months in a fog, not knowing what day it is, needing someone to feed me.

facts.chart: Directly and repeatedly asks the clinician for a specific prognosis estimate ('how long do I have'), testing for honesty and directness.
facts.says: I want you to be straight with me. No euphemisms. How long do you think I have?

facts.chart: History of hypertension and osteoarthritis, both longstanding and stable; no history of substance use disorder.
facts.says: I've had high blood pressure for years and arthritis in my knees, but nothing serious otherwise.

facts.chart: Denies any history of alcohol misuse or illicit substance use; drinks wine occasionally in the past, none in past year due to appetite loss.
facts.says: I used to enjoy a glass of wine with dinner, but I haven't had any in months - nothing appeals to me.

facts.chart: Fear of opioid addiction and of cognitive impairment ('fogginess') is the primary driver of self-restricting opioid dosing; not related to cost or access.
facts.says: It's not about money, I can afford the medicine. I'm just scared of what it will do to my mind and whether I'll get hooked.

facts.chart: Has never been started on a scheduled laxative; was not told opioids commonly cause constipation.
facts.says: Nobody told me the pain pills would do this to my stomach. I'm not taking anything regularly for my bowels.

facts.chart: Pain spikes to 9/10 two to three times daily, often in the evening, with associated difficulty sleeping.
facts.says: Some evenings it gets so bad, up to a nine, that I can't sleep at all.

facts.chart: No other close family nearby; a niece in Miami calls weekly but is not involved in caregiving.
facts.says: My niece calls from Miami every week, but she's not able to come help with day-to-day things.

facts.chart: Observes that her son appears exhausted and stressed but has not asked him how he is coping.
facts.says: My son looks so tired lately. I haven't asked him how he's really doing - I suppose I've been focused on myself.

facts.chart: Has no living will, healthcare power of attorney, or documented code status; has thought about it but 'hasn't gotten around to it.'
facts.says: I kept meaning to fill out those forms when I was still working. I never did get around to it.

facts.chart: Identifies as culturally Catholic; finds some comfort in faith but has not spoken with a priest about her diagnosis; open to spiritual care referral.
facts.says: I was raised Catholic. I haven't talked to a priest about any of this, but I wouldn't mind if someone wanted to visit.

facts.chart: Spent 28 years as a family court judge; strongly identifies with being decisive, articulate, and in control; finds loss of control over her body distressing.
facts.says: I spent twenty-eight years on the bench. I am used to being the one in control of a room, not lying in a chair waiting for someone to tell me what's happening to my own body.

facts.chart: Lives alone in a single-story home in Tampa; son visits daily after work; home has one step at entry, no other mobility hazards reported.
facts.says: I live alone in my little house. My son comes by every evening after work to check on me.

facts.chart: Reports a recent mole on her forearm that she noticed changed color slightly; unrelated to current presentation, likely benign, not urgent.
facts.says: Oh, and I noticed a little mole on my arm that seems a bit darker than before. Probably nothing, but I thought I'd mention it.

facts.chart: Has been trying ginger tea and small frequent meals on her own; mild subjective reduction in nausea with this strategy, unrelated to primary pain/constipation issue.
facts.says: My niece told me to try ginger tea and eating small meals. It does seem to help the nausea a little.

facts.chart: Son has not been given detailed prognostic information directly from oncology; patient believes he may be underestimating how serious things are.
facts.says: I don't think my son really understands how bad the scan was. I don't think anyone's spelled it out for him.

facts.chart: Has heard the word 'hospice' but has misconceptions, believing it means 'giving up' or that pain will no longer be treated.
facts.says: Hospice... isn't that just where you go to die, and they stop treating your pain? I don't really understand what that means.

facts.chart: Sleep disrupted most nights by pain and anxiety, averaging 4-5 hours with frequent waking.
facts.says: I'm lucky if I get four or five hours. Between the pain and my thoughts racing, I just can't settle.

facts.chart: Believes taking oxycodone 'as needed' means she should wait as long as possible to prove she doesn't need it, rather than treating pain proactively.
facts.says: I figure if I can go longer between doses, that proves I'm not dependent on it.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she takes oxycodone 5mg about twice a day, only when pain is unbearable.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list documents the prescribed regimen as oxycodone IR 5mg every 4 hours PRN, with a clinical note that actual use is roughly 2 doses/day - confirming significant underuse relative to the as-needed-every-4-hours order, not a dosing error by the pharmacy.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Distinguish prescribed PRN frequency from actual utilization; underdosing driven by fear of addiction/fogginess is common and should be addressed with education, not simply increasing the prescribed ceiling.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient says she was never told the pain medicine would cause constipation and is not taking anything regularly for her bowels.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list shows senna is listed as 'None currently prescribed / Not taking - No standing bowel regimen,' confirming no prophylactic laxative was ever started despite 6 weeks of opioid therapy.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Opioid-induced constipation should be anticipated and prevented with a standing bowel regimen at the time an opioid is first prescribed, not addressed only after symptoms are severe.

objectives.text: Perform a comprehensive symptom assessment (pain, constipation, mood, functional status) and identify opioid underdosing and absence of a bowel regimen as correctable contributors to poor symptom control.
Elicit the patient's private goals and values, recognizing the discordance between her wishes and her son's expressed wishes, and the fact that she has not yet disclosed her true preferences to him.

Respond to direct, repeated prognosis questions with honest, compassionate communication appropriate to a palliative care fellow's scope, using available oncology and imaging data rather than guessing or deflecting.
Identify the absence of an advance directive, surrogate decision-maker, and documented code status as an urgent care gap and plan next steps for advance care planning.
Recognize caregiver strain and a possible knowledge gap in the son's understanding of prognosis, and plan for a family meeting rather than attempting to resolve family conflict unilaterally.
Correctly identify and explain two patient-versus-chart mismatches regarding opioid use and bowel regimen, and use them as a nonjudgmental entry point for patient education.

patient.name: Ruth Castellanos
patient.language: English (fluent, occasionally references Spanish phrases from upbringing)
patient.appearance: An elegant woman with silver hair pulled back neatly, seated upright in a high-backed armchair with a crocheted throw over her lap, in a tidy living room with family photos visible on the wall behind her. Her face shows controlled discomfort and fatigue, and she maintains direct eye contact with the camera, speaking in measured, deliberate sentences even when visibly tired.

persona.personality: Formidable, precise, intellectually sharp, accustomed to authority and control; values directness and dislikes being managed or spoken down to.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks in clear, complete sentences; asks pointed, sometimes testing questions; expects direct answers and will call out vagueness or evasion.
persona.emotionalState: Composed on the surface but carrying significant private grief, fear of losing control, and unspoken sadness about family dynamics.
persona.background: Served 28 years as a family court judge in Tampa before retiring. Widowed; her late husband died eight years ago. Has one adult son, a lawyer, who is her primary caregiver, and a niece in Miami who calls weekly. Was raised in a Cuban-American Catholic family and still identifies with that heritage, though she is not currently active in a parish.
speechExamples: I want you to be straight with me. No euphemisms.
I spent twenty-eight years deciding other people's futures. I'd like a say in my own, for once.
Don't tell me what you think I want to hear. Tell me what you'd tell a colleague.
My son is a good man, but he is not ready to hear what I need to say.
I am not asking for sympathy. I am asking for information.
concerns: How much time she realistically has left
Whether she can stay at home instead of being hospitalized
How to tell her son she wants to stop treatment without devastating him
Whether increasing her pain medication will make her mentally foggy or dependent
Whether stopping chemotherapy means her pain will no longer be treated

scenario.studentBrief: You are a palliative care fellow conducting a telehealth consult with Ruth Castellanos, a 77-year-old retired judge with metastatic pancreatic cancer, referred by her oncologist for symptom management and goals-of-care discussion after her recent CT showed disease progression despite three cycles of chemotherapy. Review her chart before the visit; she is expecting a direct conversation.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Uncontrolled upper abdominal pain and uncertainty about pursuing further chemotherapy after disease progression
scenario.openingLine: My oncologist sent me to see you. I have this pain in my stomach that goes to my back, and frankly, I'm not sure what I want to do next about the chemotherapy.
tasks: Take a focused history of her pain and other symptoms, and review her current medication use
Explore her understanding of her illness and elicit her personal goals and values
Respond to her questions about prognosis using available information
Review advance care planning status and discuss next steps
Assess caregiver support and discuss options for family communication

answerKey.primaryProblem: Poorly controlled cancer pain and opioid-induced constipation in a patient with progressive metastatic pancreatic cancer (ECOG 3), compounded by unaddressed goals-of-care discordance with family and absence of advance care planning.
differential: Undertreated nociceptive visceral pain due to patient-driven opioid underdosing from fear of addiction/sedation (primary explanation)
Opioid-induced constipation vs. malignant bowel obstruction (less likely given no vomiting, no distension beyond mild bloating, no biliary dilation on CT)
Depression/demoralization related to functional decline and anticipatory grief vs. major depressive disorder requiring psychiatric referral
Hepatic capsular pain from new liver metastases contributing to right upper quadrant component of pain
keyFindings: Pain 7/10 constant, breakthrough to 9/10, poorly controlled due to self-restricted oxycodone use (2 doses/day instead of prescribed q4h PRN)
No bowel movement in 5 days with no standing laxative ever started despite 6 weeks of opioid therapy
ECOG 3 functional decline with 9 kg weight loss over 10 weeks, consistent with disease progression shown on CT (new hepatic metastases)
No advance directive, surrogate, or documented code status on file

Significant goals-of-care discordance: patient privately wishes to stop chemotherapy and prioritize comfort at home, but has not disclosed this to her son, who is advocating for continued aggressive treatment
Caregiver strain in son, who may not have full prognostic understanding
Fears about opioids (addiction, cognitive fogginess) driving dangerous underdosing and unnecessary suffering
plan: Provide patient education correcting misconceptions about PRN opioid dosing: encourage proactive, scheduled or appropriately frequent dosing of oxycodone for better pain control, with reassurance about low addiction risk in cancer pain and strategies to monitor for sedation

Initiate a standing bowel regimen (e.g., stimulant laxative) for opioid-induced constipation prevention/treatment, per standard palliative bowel protocol, and consider further workup if constipation does not resolve or red flags develop (coordinate with primary oncology/PCP for any needed in-person exam or imaging if obstruction is suspected)

Use direct, honest, values-based communication to answer her prognosis question, acknowledging uncertainty while giving a realistic timeframe range based on functional decline and progressive metastatic disease, avoiding false reassurance or evasion

Explore and document her illness understanding and goals using a structured goals-of-care framework (e.g., 'what matters most'), and support her in considering how and when to share her wishes with her son

Flag the absence of an advance directive/healthcare surrogate/code status as an urgent action item; offer to facilitate completion of advance directive documentation and code status discussion within scope of palliative care practice

Recommend and offer to help convene a family meeting with the son (and patient's permission) to align understanding of prognosis and treatment goals, rather than attempting to mediate the conflict without the son present
Screen for and address caregiver burden; offer resources (e.g., social work referral, respite care information) for the son
Offer referral to chaplaincy/spiritual care given her Catholic background and openness to spiritual support

Communicate findings and recommendations back to the oncology team regarding goals of care prior to any decision on second-line chemotherapy, respecting that the chemotherapy decision itself remains within oncology's scope
redFlags: No advance directive or documented code status in a patient with rapidly progressive, life-limiting illness and clear decline in performance status
Severe, escalating pain being significantly undertreated due to patient self-restriction, risking unnecessary suffering and crisis presentation
Unresolved, unspoken discordance between patient's wishes and family expectations, risking a crisis-driven or conflicted decision-making process later
5 days of constipation in a patient with abdominal malignancy warrants exclusion of bowel obstruction if it does not respond promptly to laxative therapy or if vomiting/worsening distension develops
educationPoints: Fear of addiction and of cognitive clouding are common, often unspoken barriers to adequate opioid use in cancer pain and should be proactively asked about and addressed with education
Opioid-induced constipation should be anticipated and prevented with a standing bowel regimen whenever an opioid is started, not treated reactively after days of symptoms

Patients and family members may hold divergent goals; the clinician's role is to create a safe space for the patient to clarify and voice her own values, and to facilitate family communication rather than to decide or mediate unilaterally without the family present
Direct, honest answers to prognosis questions, calibrated to the patient's communication style and expressed desire for directness, build trust more effectively than vague reassurance
Common misconceptions about hospice (e.g., that it means pain will no longer be treated, or that it equals 'giving up') should be gently explored and corrected as part of informed decision-making

Advance care planning (surrogate designation, code status, living will) should be addressed proactively, especially when a care gap like this is identified, and is within the core scope of palliative care practice

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in Tampa, Florida, seated in her living room
profile.summary: A 77-year-old retired judge with metastatic pancreatic cancer and newly progressive hepatic metastases presents for a palliative care telehealth consult with undertreated cancer pain (self-restricted opioid dosing from fear of addiction/fogginess), untreated opioid-induced constipation, and a hidden discordance between her private wish to stop chemotherapy and focus on comfort versus her son's wish for her to continue fighting. The case teaches symptom assessment and correction of opioid-related misconceptions, skilled exploration of goals and values, direct prognostic communication, identification of an advance care planning gap, and recognition that family conflict should be addressed through a facilitated family meeting rather than unilateral mediation.
profile.title: Goals-of-Care Conversation and Symptom Review in Progressive Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer
